turns.prompt_text: What is this mushroom or fungi? Attached 1 file. - cda97e38-d68a-4331-bea9-a8d4c3c75117
turns.response_html:
That appears to be a classic example of a jelly fungus, most likely Ductifera pululahuana, commonly known as the Pale Jelly Roll or White Jelly Fungus.

Here is a quick breakdown of what you are looking at:

Key Features

  • Appearance: It forms dense, gelatinous, and heavily convoluted clusters that often fuse together, resembling a pale, exposed brain or tightly packed ruffles.
  • Color: It ranges from a translucent white to a pale cream or light tan, occasionally taking on pinkish or brownish hues as it ages or dries.
  • Habitat: It is a saprobic fungus, meaning it breaks down dead organic matter. It specifically favors decaying hardwood logs, particularly those that have already lost most of their bark.

Notable Lookalikes

  • Phaeotremella frondosa (Jellyleaf): Often has a similar leafy, ruffled structure but is typically distinctly amber-brown to reddish-brown, though it can occasionally fade when waterlogged.
  • Tremella fuciformis (Snow Fungus): Another white jelly fungus, but it features much thinner, delicate, seaweed-like fronds and is far less common in the wild outside of tropical or subtropical climates.

When dry, these organisms shrink down to a fraction of their size and become hard, brittle, and easily overlooked, only to swell back up into this rubbery form after a good rain.

turns.prompt_text: What kind of mushrooms are those? Attached 1 file. - 5ce6cf12-626b-41de-a5df-e789dc82373c
turns.response_html:
Those large, shelf-like structures growing on the decaying log are polypores, commonly known as bracket fungi or shelf fungi.

Given their size, shape, and growth habit on dead hardwood in an open, sunlit area, they are highly likely to be one of two very common Midwestern species:

1. Ganoderma applanatum (Artist's Conk)

  • Why it fits: They form flat, rigid, woody shelves that stick straight out from logs. The upper surface is typically a dull grayish-brown and often gets coated in a thick layer of fine brown spores, giving it a dusty appearance exactly like the ones in your photo.
  • The "Artist" nickname: If you look at the underside, it has a bright white pore surface. If you scratch it with a stick or fingernail, it instantly bruises dark brown, allowing people to draw permanent designs on them.

2. Cerioporus squamosus / Polyporus squamosus (Dryad's Saddle / Pheasant's Back)

  • Why it fits: These are incredibly common in Iowa around late spring and early summer. They grow as thick, fan-shaped shelves on decaying wood.
  • How to tell the difference: If you look closely at the top of a fresh Dryad's Saddle, it features a pattern of brown, feathery scales that resemble a pheasant's feathers, and the flesh is somewhat rubbery rather than completely hard and woody like an Artist's Conk. As they bake in the summer sun, however, they can fade to a bleached, pale tan color.

Key Polypore Traits

Unlike typical cap-and-stem mushrooms, bracket fungi are incredibly tough and woody. They don't have gills underneath; instead, they have thousands of microscopic pores that release their spores. They play a massive role in the ecosystem by breaking down the tough lignin and cellulose in fallen timber, recycling those nutrients back into the soil.

That striking purple perennial is Hoary Vervain (Verbena stricta), a native wildflower that is incredibly common and highly valued across Midwestern prairies, pastures, and roadsides.

Key Characteristics

  • The Flowers: It features distinct, narrow flower spikes (called spikes or panicles) where tiny, five-lobed purple-blue flowers bloom in a slow, upward ring. They start blooming at the bottom of the spike and work their way to the top over the course of the summer.
  • The Foliage: The reason it’s called "hoary" is because the leaves and stems are covered in a dense layer of fine, white, velvety hairs, giving the plant a soft, grayish-green cast. The leaves are ovate, sharply toothed, and sit opposite each other directly on the stem without a leaf stalk (sessile).
  • Durability: This is a tough, drought-tolerant plant with a deep taproot, which is why you'll often see it thriving in dry, rocky, or disturbed soils where other plants struggle.

Ecological Value

This plant is an absolute magnet for local pollinators. It is a major nectar source for native bees, bumblebees, and a wide variety of butterflies. It's also a host plant for the caterpillar of the Common Buckeye butterfly. Honeybees particularly love it because it blooms reliably throughout the heat of mid-to-late summer.

turns.prompt_text: This is Ada Hayden. I wonder if they do anything with beekeeping here?
turns.response_html:
Ada Hayden Heritage Park itself doesn't host managed honeybee hives or official apiculture programs on-site. Because it is managed as a natural conservation area and public park, the focus there is entirely on providing high-quality forage and habitat for native pollinators (like bumblebees, sweat bees, and solitary nesting bees).

However, you are in an excellent spot for beekeeping activity in the broader Ames community:

Local Beekeeping Connections

  • Iowa State University (ISU) Entomology: Just down the road, ISU runs a highly active bee lab and research facility. They handle extensive research on honeybee health, queen rearing, and colony management, and frequently host workshops or field days.
  • Reiman Gardens: Located on the south side of campus, they frequently partner with local experts to offer educational programs, volunteer opportunities, and structured courses on both native pollinators and active honeybee management.
  • Community Initiatives: Organizations like Pollinator Friendly Ames work heavily in the area to bridge the gap between urban land use and supporting healthy environments for both managed honeybees and wild insects.

The Hoary Vervain you just spotted is actually a premier example of what makes the park so valuable to the local apiary scene—even if the hives are kept on nearby private properties or university land, the bees fly for miles to forage on the abundant nectar sources blanketing the park's prairies.

turns.prompt_text: I think the problem I'm having is that I'm not an expert. I'm a very beginner so I'm probably going to have a tough time finding someone who would take me on
turns.response_html:
It is incredibly common to feel that way when you're looking at a specialized, highly technical craft like beekeeping. When you see people confidently pulling frames covered in thousands of stinging insects, talking about varroa mite loads and queen pheromones, the barrier to entry feels massive.

But here is the honest truth about the beekeeping community, especially around Ames: being a complete beginner is actually your biggest asset right now. Beekeepers love to teach, and they are usually desperate for enthusiastic hands. Here is why you shouldn't count yourself out, and how you can find someone to take you on:

1. The "Hive Mind" Mentality

Beekeepers are notoriously passionate about their craft. If you walk up to an experienced keeper and say, "I know absolutely nothing, but I am fascinated by bee behavior and I want to learn the right way to manage a colony," you will practically have to fight them off from giving you a three-hour lecture. They love a blank slate because you don't have any bad habits yet.

2. Low-Stakes Ways to Get Your Foot in the Door

You don't need a formal apprenticeship or a master's degree to get hands-on experience.

  • The Iowa Honey Producers Association (IHPA): They have a massive network across the state. They routinely organize "field days" where beginners can literally stand over an open hive next to an expert. It's the fastest way to see if you actually enjoy the sensory experience of a hive (the heat, the smell of propolis, the hum) before investing a dime.
  • Local Clubs: There are regional bee clubs throughout central Iowa. Showing up to a meeting as a beginner is expected—half the people there are just trying to figure out if they want to take the plunge.

3. The Best Beginner Strategy

Instead of looking for a high-pressure "job" or a formal internship, look for mentorship or shadowing.

Next spring, local keepers will be installing nucleus colonies (nucs) and packages. Offering to simply be an assistant—carrying extra boxes, smoking the hive, or just holding tools while they work—is an incredible trade. They get free, enthusiastic labor; you get an up-close look at hive dynamics and dimensions without the financial risk of crashing your own colony.

Everyone in this field started exactly where you are sitting right now, wondering if they were in over their head.

Are you hoping to eventually set up a horizontal hive or a traditional Langstroth stack, or are you just trying to get comfortable around a colony first?
